notes.text: God is like **a shield** to Abram since he protects him. or [I protect you like a shield] or [I will shield you]

The phrase **son of the inheritance** is used here as a common expression meaning “inheritor” or “heir”; it does not refer to an actual son. Consider whether or not your language has a similar expression. or [Because when I die, the one who will own]

In the Hebrew text, Abram emphasizes the fact that Eliezer was from Damascus, which means he was a foreigner from a foreign city, not a blood relative. Consider what is the best way to communicate that in your language. Also, note how you translated “the city of Damascus” in Genesis 14:15.
Some languages omit these words because the same speaker is still speaking to the same audience.
In the Hebrew text **to me** is before **you have given no seed** to emphasize Abram’s lack of an heir related to him. [you have given no offspring to me]
It may be necessary to translate it differently here because of the different context.
The phrase **comes from your bowels** is a common expression that refers to fathering a child. Make sure your translation of this clause does not imply that Abram would give birth to a son.

notes.topic: Abram was probably inside a tent
notes.text: Abram was probably inside a tent, not inside a house. But if possible, it is best to leave this implied in a translation (as the Hebrew text does).

Throughout this chapter, make sure it is clear in your translation who is speaking to whom. Always use pronouns and nouns in a way that is clear and natural in your language. or [So as Abram looked up at the stars, Yahweh told him]

Notice that Yahweh, referred to as **he**, is now the subject again. Make sure it is clear in your translation who is speaking to whom here and throughout this section. or [and because of that, Yahweh reckoned Abram to be righteous] or [so Yahweh considered Abram to have a right relationship with him]
Make sure it is clear in your translation that Abram is the one speaking here, not Yahweh. or [But he asked Yahweh]

This phrase refers to large birds that eat dead animal meat. Examples of these birds include vultures, buzzards, condors, eagles, and crows. or [Then some vultures swooped down and landed] or [Then some meat-eating birds]
or [terrible misery and fear came upon Abram]

For emphasis in the Hebrew text, Moses places the pronoun **you** in an emphatic position in the sentence (before the verb) to change the topic. This adds emphasis to what he is saying. If your language uses explicit pronouns for emphasis, you may want to use that construction in your translation. Other languages may have other ways of bringing out this emphasis. Do what is clear and natural in your language.

This Hebrew word for **darkness** implies that it was darker than normal, so that not even light from the moon and stars was visible. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.
To **cut a covenant** means to make a covenant. The terminology refers to ancient rituals around making covenants, which is illustrated in Genesis 15. See the imagery and how you translated there.
In the Hebrew text, **To your offspring** is first in this quote to emphasize Abram’s descendants. or [I hereby give this land to your offspring]
This phrase probably refers to the Wadi El-Arish (not the Nile River), which is on the border between Egypt and Israel. It is best in a translation to leave this general, as the Hebrew text does.
